## Context

On CPU and small-GPU laptops, decode is the second half of the latency budget and it is the half nobody optimises. Speculative decoding pairs the resident model with a small draft model that guesses several tokens ahead; the target verifies them in one pass. Published measurements range from 1.4x to 3.2x wall-clock generation (64 t/s → 206 t/s for a 26B target with a 2B-class draft; roughly 2x on an M1 Ultra), at identical output when sampling is greedy.

It is also a trap if enabled blindly: the same reports show a draft depth above the default of 3 making generation *slower*, and a Vulkan/UMA iGPU regression where the draft model's per-token time collapsed by five orders of magnitude. So this lands as an opt-in, measured, and refused-on-this-hardware-when-it-is-slower feature — not a default.

## What to change

- A probe on the runtime: does it expose a draft model at all? Ollama does not, so this ships as a documented `llama-server` path alongside the existing provider, with no silent switch.
- A bench script that measures decode t/s with and without the draft at depths 3/5/8 on this machine and writes the result into `readiness` output.
- Enable only when the measured speedup is at least 1.3x; otherwise the panel says "draft model measured slower on this machine" and leaves it off.
- A greedy-identity check: the same prompt at temperature 0 must produce the same answer with and without speculation.
- `docs/GUIDE.md`: the memory cost (a second model in RAM/VRAM), how to turn it off, and which hardware classes are known-bad.

**Safety:** opt-in, local only, and it never downloads a model on its own. The confirmation step names the extra memory before the setting is saved. Speculation changes how tokens are produced, never which tool may run: the risk tiers and approval gate are untouched.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — every token is one forward pass of one model, so decode speed is whatever the model and hardware give (reference range: 1.4x-3.2x available on hardware where the draft predicts well)
- **Target:** decode tokens/second up **40% or more** on the committed bench prompts with output identical to the no-draft run at temperature 0, and the extra memory reported before the setting can be enabled
- **Must not regress:** the answer must be identical (greedy) or within the existing eval's noise band at temperature 0.4; time-to-first-token may not rise more than 5%; a machine where the probe measures a slowdown must end up with the feature off

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The probe measures this machine and refuses to enable a configuration that is slower
- [ ] Greedy output is identical with and without the draft on the bench prompt set
- [ ] Decode t/s, draft depth and extra memory are recorded and shown before enabling
- [ ] The feature is off by default and documented as unavailable on Ollama's API
- [ ] Nothing is downloaded, and no provider may be swapped silently

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/router.test.js test/agent.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
```

## Time estimate

~1 week

items.title: perf(agent): run independent read-tier tool calls concurrently
items.verify:
node --test test/agent.test.js test/tools.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
items.body:
## Context

`src/agent.js` executes tool calls in a strict `for` loop over `out.toolCalls`, so a turn that reads three files, greps a directory and checks the time pays five round trips for work that has no ordering between it. Models emit these batches because the answer needs all of them; the loop then serialises them anyway.

Top coding agents fan work out and bring back only the conclusion. For a single-user local assistant the same principle applies at a smaller scale: parallelise the reads, never the actions.

## What to change

- Classify each emitted call with the existing `src/risk.js` tiers, then run the whole `read` batch concurrently with a small fixed cap (4) and re-emit results to the model in the original call order.
- The batch stops being parallel the moment an `act` or `blocked` call appears: those run alone, in order, through the existing approval gate.
- An unknown or unclassifiable tool is treated as `act` for scheduling purposes — serialised — so a new plugin cannot inherit concurrency by accident.
- `src/telemetry.js`: record tool wall-clock, per-call and for the batch, so the win is visible.

**Safety:** concurrency is a scheduling change, not a permission change. Only calls already classified `read` may overlap; approvals remain sequential, single-use, and answered one at a time, and a failure in one read aborts the rest rather than letting a half-batch look complete.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** sequential — `src/agent.js` runs `for (const call of out.toolCalls)`, so N independent reads cost N round trips and a 3-file turn pays 3x the wall clock
- **Target:** wall clock down **35% or more** on the committed multi-read turn suite (N >= 3 reads), with identical model-visible results in identical order
- **Must not regress:** no `act` call may ever run concurrently or out of order; approval prompts stay one-at-a-time; a denied or failed call still produces the same typed failure; transcript order stays deterministic

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Read-tier calls run concurrently with a cap of 4 and results are re-ordered to match the model's call order
- [ ] Any `act`, `blocked` or unrecognised tool forces the batch back to serial
- [ ] A failure in one call cancels the others and is reported as one typed failure
- [ ] The multi-read suite shows a 35%+ wall-clock reduction with no behavioural difference
- [ ] Telemetry records per-call and per-batch durations

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/agent.test.js test/tools.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
```

## Time estimate

~4-6 days

items.title: perf(brain): cut over to the next backend when the first token is late
items.verify:
node --test test/router.test.js test/voice-latency.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
items.body:
## Context

`docs/ROUTING.md` says a backend that "accepted, then silent" is classified `TIMEOUT` and the chain falls through — and that is true, but only once `TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` in `src/brain.js:21` expires. `ResilientRouter.run()` (`src/router.js:40`) leaves a backend only when its `chat()` throws; nothing watches *when the first token arrives*. On the hardware this product actually runs on, the commonest real failure is exactly that silence — a cold model load, a VRAM swap caused by another application, a wedged `ollama serve` — so the turn waits up to three minutes before the second candidate in the plan is even tried. `src/telemetry.js:53` already writes down the budget this violates: `firstTokenMs`, target **700 ms**.

The general problem was solved by somebody else first. *The Tail at Scale* describes **hedged requests**: issue the request, and when it has not answered by the p95 latency, issue it again somewhere else and take the winner. Routing decides *which* model answers the turn (`mind-03`); a deadline decides *when to stop waiting for it*. Cascades such as FrugalGPT escalate only after a complete cheap answer exists, which the same literature names as the reason cascades are a poor fit for interactive tails: the fixed cost is a whole generation, not one token.

## What to change

- A per-attempt first-token timer in `ResilientRouter`, started when `backend.chat()` is called rather than when text appears. When it fires with nothing emitted, abort that attempt (pass an `AbortSignal` through to the provider) and move to the next candidate exactly as a thrown `TIMEOUT` does today.
- `FIRST_TOKEN_DEADLINE_MS` in `src/config.js`, default **1200**, with a per-backend override; `0` restores today's behaviour exactly.
- The timer exists only when there is somewhere to cut over to. On a single-provider install (`LLM_FALLBACK` empty) no timer is created and nothing can be aborted, so the default turn is unchanged.
- Record the cutover in the attempt trail (`{ backend, deadlineMs, ms, cutover: true }`) and therefore in `lastRoute`, so the panel and `npm run health` can say "the local model had produced no token after 1.2 s; this turn finished on the fallback" instead of showing a turn that merely took a while.
- `docs/ROUTING.md`: a short section on the three ways a backend can fail — refused, rejected, silent — and which one the deadline exists for.

## What this is not

Written down because these were proposed alongside it and rejected on measurements rather than taste:

- **Querying every installed model and letting a judge pick.** On one laptop GPU the candidates compete for the same memory: every model after the first costs a swap-in (5–30 s by the proposal's own numbers) and the judge adds another generation. It is the most expensive verifier available, and it is being asked to improve latency.
- **Keeping three or four specialist models resident "hot".** That is a multi-GPU property. `docs/COMPETITIVE-FRONTIER.md` §10 already refuses "a second resident model for everything" because memory on a personal laptop is the scarce resource.
- **A `[PASS]` first token, where the small model declares it cannot answer.** That is a self-reported confidence signal, and the routing literature is explicit that those are poorly calibrated: a model that says `PASS` wrongly pays a needless escalation on every easy turn, and one that never says it makes the mechanism dead weight. If `mind-03`'s eval shows a routing gap that no code-checkable signal can close, this returns with a measured false-accept rate to defend — not before.

**Safety:** a cutover can only cross a boundary the person already opted into. It cannot invent a hop: with no `LLM_FALLBACK` there is no second candidate and no timer. It never fires after a delta has been handed to the caller (the `STREAM_CUT` rule at `src/router.js:84` stays intact), and it never abandons a model that has produced a token — a slow generator keeps its turn.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** `src/brain.js:21` allows a silent backend **180,000 ms** before the turn falls through, so the fallback's entire benefit sits behind a three-minute wait; `ResilientRouter` leaves a backend only on a thrown error, and nothing measures or enforces the 700 ms `firstTokenMs` target recorded in `src/telemetry.js:53`
- **Target:** a turn whose primary produces no first token cuts over at the configured deadline — default **1200 ms**, p95 within 100 ms of it — taking the silent-backend worst case from **180,000 ms** to **deadline + one hop**, and holding `firstTokenMs` p95 for dead-primary turns **under 3 s** on the recorded baseline script
- **Must not regress:** zero cutovers after a delta is emitted (the existing `test/router.test.js` case "a failure after text reached the caller is not retried anywhere" stays green), zero timers and zero aborts on a single-backend install, zero cutovers on a model that has produced at least one token, and task success on the `mind-03` eval unchanged — a deadline may never trade an answer for speed

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `FIRST_TOKEN_DEADLINE_MS=0` reproduces today's behaviour exactly, asserted by test
- [ ] A backend that never emits a token is abandoned at the deadline and the next candidate answers the turn
- [ ] A backend that emits one token and then stalls is never abandoned (STREAM_CUT preserved)
- [ ] A single-backend plan creates no timer and aborts nothing
- [ ] The cutover is visible in the attempt trail, `lastRoute` and `npm run health`
- [ ] The recorded run shows `firstTokenMs` p95 under 3 s on a dead primary

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/router.test.js test/voice-latency.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
```

Use a fake backend that never resolves plus an injected clock, the pattern `test/router.test.js` already uses. No real model and no network are required to prove any of the above.

## Time estimate

~3-4 days.

items.title: feat(voice): full duplex on the laptop CPU, with no GPU in the loop
items.body:
## Context

Moshi's 160-200 ms duplex demo is the number everyone quotes, and it runs on a GPU with a speech model that owns both directions. That is not the machine a personal assistant lives on. Every hosted stack (LiveKit, Pipecat) is fast because a datacentre is doing the work; every local stack is turn-based because taking a turn is the cheap way to be correct.

## What to change

- A single loop that listens while it speaks: the microphone stays open during playback, the playback is cancelled sample-accurately, and the endpoint decision is made from local features only.
- An explicit CPU budget: the always-on path may use at most a quarter of one core, and the budget is measured by a script, not asserted in prose.
- An honest degradation path: when the machine cannot hold the budget, the loop falls back to half-duplex and says so in the UI instead of glitching.
- `docs/VOICE.md`: what is lost against a GPU duplex model, in the same table as what is gained.

**Safety:** barge-in must silence the assistant within 150 ms and must never send audio anywhere. The fallback to half-duplex is a feature, not a failure — but it has to be visible.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — the loop is turn-based: listening stops when speaking starts, so there is no barge-in to measure; CPU cost of the idle path is the recogniser's own cost
- **Target:** barge-in to silence in 150 ms or less, endpoint p50 at 250 ms or less, CPU at or below 25% of one core while listening, resident memory at or below 600 MB, zero network bytes
- **Must not regress:** must not regress the cut-off rate, the WER measured by `voice-05`, or the approval gate: nothing spoken by the assistant can approve an action

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Barge-in silences playback in 150 ms or less on a named reference laptop, measured 20 times
- [ ] The CPU budget is enforced by a test that fails when the listening path exceeds it
- [ ] Falling back to half-duplex is visible in the UI and recorded in telemetry
- [ ] No audio, partial transcript or embedding leaves the machine on this path

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/voice.test.js test/audio-input.test.js
node scripts/bench-voice.js --cpu-budget
```

## Time estimate

~3-4 weeks

items.title: feat(desktop): ground on the accessibility tree before spending a model on pixels
items.body:
## Context

UI-TARS showed that a vision-language model can point at a control, and the field took that as the answer to GUI control. It is the expensive answer: a screenshot plus a model call per click, on a machine that already publishes a structured tree of every control it is showing. A laptop has an accessibility API. Using it first is faster, cheaper, works when the window is occluded, and — unlike a coordinate — it can be replayed tomorrow.

## What to change

- A resolver that takes a spoken target ("the Save button", "the third row", "the Wi-Fi toggle") and matches it against the accessibility tree of the focused window.
- A stable selector for every resolved control — role plus name plus path — so an approved action can be replayed and verified rather than re-predicted.
- The pixel path as a documented fallback, used only when the tree has nothing to match, and labelled as unverified in the trace.
- `docs/DESKTOP-ACCESSIBILITY.md`: what the tree exposes on each supported platform, and what it does not.

**Safety:** resolving a control must never click it. The preview shows the matched control's role, name and window, and the approval gate is unchanged.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — no accessibility-tree reader; screen control is one screenshot plus a model call, and nothing can be replayed without asking a model again
- **Target:** zero model calls when the target is named in the accessibility tree, grounding p50 at 120 ms or less, 95% or better element accuracy on the bench from `lead-06`, with the pixel fallback rate reported
- **Must not regress:** must not regress the approval gate, must not act on an ambiguous match (report it instead), and must not claim success for a click that was never verified

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A named control resolves without a model call, proven by request count
- [ ] Two controls with the same name are reported as ambiguous, never picked arbitrarily
- [ ] Every resolved control has a stable selector that survives a window restart
- [ ] The pixel fallback is visible in the trace with reason `no a11y match`

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/desktop.test.js test/verify.test.js
node scripts/bench-grounding.js
```

## Time estimate

~2-3 weeks

items.title: feat(agent): carry the read-back through to the reply, the API and the export
items.body:
## Context

`skill-02` made an action's success a fact with three states instead of a boolean. That fact currently lives in the trace and in one warning line. A product that leads on honesty has to put it everywhere the claim goes: the reply, the API response, the UI, and the exported record — otherwise the only person who sees the difference is a developer reading logs.

## What to change

- A visible marker per action in the conversation view: verified, contradicted, unverified — with the read-back text on hover.
- An API field that a script can assert on, so the verification is testable by anyone, not just visible.
- Reply language rules enforced in code: a contradicted action may not be described with past-tense success, whichever model produced the words.
- The export includes verification records, and an audit command reports the ratio of verified to unverified actions in a period.

**Safety:** verification never upgrades a claim. A missing record is `unverified`, not `verified`, and export must not fabricate a status it did not record.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** verification exists in the trace only (`src/verify.js`, 20-case fault-injection suite, 0 silent wrong successes); replies, API and export carry nothing
- **Target:** 100% of act-tier actions carry a three-state record in reply, API and export; 0 replies describe a contradicted action as done across a 20-case language suite; p95 added latency at or below 5 ms
- **Must not regress:** must not regress reply latency, must not leak verification detail into a channel where it was never computed, and must not turn an unverified action into a verified one on export

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The UI shows the three states distinguishably, including for colour-blind users
- [ ] A script can read the verification status from the API without scraping HTML
- [ ] A contradicted action is never described as complete, tested against a model that tries
- [ ] Export round-trips the status and the audit reports the ratio

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/verify.test.js test/http-surface.test.js test/export-cost.test.js
```

## Time estimate

~1 week

items.title: feat(agent): write the undo record before the action, not after it
items.body:
## Context

OpenAdapt's best idea is that a program stops when reality does not match what it recorded. The idea it does not have is the inverse: nothing in this category can undo an action it already took. A journal written *after* a successful action cannot help when the action succeeds and the process dies before the write — which is exactly the case a user needs it for.

## What to change

- A journal entry created before the action runs: what is about to change, the previous value if one exists, and how to restore it.
- Undo as a first-class conversational verb ("undo that"), routed through the same approval gate as the original action.
- A visible journal the user can inspect and prune, with entries linked to the trace id of the action that created them.
- Honest per-tool capability: a tool that cannot be undone records that fact instead of pretending.

**Safety:** undo is itself an action: it previews what it will restore and asks. A journal entry is never written by a model's description of what it did — only by the tool that did it.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — `laptop-05` plans an undo journal for file actions; there is no pre-action record today, and a crashed action leaves nothing to reverse
- **Target:** 100% of act-tier actions have a journal entry written before execution, undo restores a verified state in 95% of 20 scenarios, p95 overhead at or below 20 ms per action
- **Must not regress:** must not regress approval coverage or action latency, and must not report an action as undone when the read-back disagrees

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Killing the process between action and reply still leaves a usable journal entry
- [ ] Undo of a write restores byte-identical previous content, verified by read-back
- [ ] A tool without undo support says so in the preview, before approval
- [ ] The journal is inspectable and prunable without reading JSON by hand

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/journal.test.js test/agent.test.js test/verify.test.js
```

## Time estimate

~2 weeks

items.title: feat(skills): teach a routine by talking, and fold a mid-run correction into it
items.body:
## Context

OpenAdapt compiles a program from a demonstration you record with a mouse. OpenClaw gives you prose a model re-reads. Neither can be taught the way a person teaches a colleague: do it once while talking, then say "no, the other window" and have the correction become part of the routine. That is a conversation-shaped interface to a compiled program, and it is the piece nobody ships.

## What to change

- A teach mode: the approved trace of a successful run becomes a named skill, with the spoken description as its trigger phrase.
- A correction path: when the user redirects mid-run, the difference between the approved and corrected step is shown as a diff and, on approval, folded into the skill.
- A rule that a skill never learns silently — every mutation is a visible, approved diff with a version number.
- Unlearn: deleting a skill that a schedule references is refused with the reason, not silently broken.

**Safety:** a correction is an approval, not an inference. The diff is shown in words the user can judge, and a skill that cannot be described in one sentence is refused rather than taught.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — no skill format, no teach mode, no way to express a correction; `skill-01` compiles and replays, it does not learn
- **Target:** a correction produces an approved diff in 90% or more of 15 scripted scenarios, replay p50 stays under 300 ms after mutation, and 0 skills mutate without an approved diff
- **Must not regress:** must not regress replay determinism or the approval gate, and a rejected correction must leave the skill byte-identical

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A taught skill runs with zero model calls and a byte-identical trace
- [ ] A correction is shown as a diff before it is applied
- [ ] A rejected correction leaves the stored skill unchanged, proven by hash
- [ ] Deleting a referenced skill is refused with a message naming the schedule

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/skill.test.js test/repair.test.js test/agent.test.js
```

## Time estimate

~3 weeks

items.title: bench(desktop): publish a reproducible bench for voice-driven laptop control
items.body:
## Context

Every claim in this category is incomparable. UI-TARS reports OSWorld, OpenAdapt reports one OpenEMR workflow, Moshi reports a latency figure on a GPU, and nobody reports what happens when the assistant is wrong. A category leader is the project that makes its claims checkable by someone who does not trust it — and that means a bench anyone can run, with the failure modes in it.

## What to change

- 40 tasks over five shapes: read-only questions, single reversible actions, multi-step routines, a task that must be refused, and a task that must be undone.
- Four measurements per task: success, wall-clock latency, whether approval was requested exactly once, and whether the read-back verified the outcome.
- A deterministic dry-run mode that exercises the harness without touching a real desktop, so CI can run it.
- Published results per release, with the machine named and the raw JSON committed.

**Safety:** the bench never runs destructive tasks against a real machine without a disposable profile, and a refused task counts as success only when the refusal is the correct outcome.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — no bench; the repository's claims about desktop control are supported by unit tests, not by task measurements
- **Target:** 40 tasks complete in 5 minutes or less on a reference laptop, dry-run deterministic across 3 runs, and a published table with success, p50 latency, approval coverage and verification rate
- **Must not regress:** must not regress CI duration by more than 60 seconds, and every published number must be reproducible from the committed config

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A stranger can run the bench and get the published numbers, on the named machine
- [ ] Refused tasks and undone tasks are scored, not skipped
- [ ] Approval coverage is measured per task, not asserted globally
- [ ] The dry-run mode is safe enough to run in CI

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/bench.test.js
node scripts/bench-desktop.js --dry-run --json
```

## Time estimate

~2 weeks

items.title: feat(memory): remember what was done, not only what was said
items.body:
## Context

Ask any assistant "what did we do about the invoice?" and it will search its transcript, which is a record of sentences, not of actions. The interesting memory is the trace: which file was written, which reminder was set, which skill was compiled, and whether it verified. Every competitor indexes the conversation; none indexes the work.

## What to change

- A bounded index of executed actions: tool, arguments digest, verification status, outcome, trace id — searchable by the same local search the history uses.
- Answers that cite a trace id, so "we renamed the file on Tuesday" can be checked against the action that did it.
- Retention rules shared with the existing retention plan: the index obeys the same deletion policy as the transcript.
- No model summarising on the write path — the index stores facts, and a summary is generated only when asked.

**Safety:** the index must never contain tool output verbatim (secrets and file contents), only a digest and a short human summary the tool itself reported.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — history search covers transcripts only; there is no action index, so "what did you do" is answered from what the assistant said it did
- **Target:** 90% recall@5 on 40 questions about past actions, p50 at 250 ms or less, and 0 answers that cite an action which does not exist
- **Must not regress:** must not regress transcript search, must not store tool output containing secrets, and must not answer from the index when the trace says the action was contradicted

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A question about a past action returns the trace id and the verification status
- [ ] Deleting a conversation removes its actions from the index
- [ ] An answer never cites an action id that is absent from the store
- [ ] Index size stays bounded — the plan states the cap and prunes oldest-first

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/memory.test.js test/retention-plan.test.js
```

## Time estimate

~2 weeks

items.title: fix(agent): make an approval single-use, session-bound and expiring
items.body:
## Context

OpenClaw reaches twenty chat channels, which is genuinely good. Breadth without discipline is how an approval becomes a hole: a prompt raised in one session, answered in another, replayed by a third, is not consent. This product's entire differentiator is the gate, so the gate has to be the strongest thing in the codebase rather than the most convenient.

## What to change

- An approval record keyed by session, channel and the exact action digest: a different action, a different session or a different channel cannot satisfy it.
- Single use, with a 10-minute expiry that is enforced rather than advisory, and a cancellation path when the requester disconnects.
- An audit line per approval: what was asked, by whom, from which channel, and what happened next.
- A test suite of adversarial cases — replay, cross-session, cross-channel, expired, and forged id.

**Safety:** a refused or expired approval must fail closed and leave nothing executed; a forged id must be indistinguishable from an unknown one in the reply.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** approvals are held in memory keyed by id only, with a 10-minute timeout; replay and cross-session satisfaction are not tested
- **Target:** 0 of 20 adversarial cases satisfy an approval out of band, expiry enforced to within 1 second, 100% of approvals produce an audit line
- **Must not regress:** must not regress the interactive approval flow or its latency, and must not make a legitimate approval harder to give

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Replaying an old approval id executes nothing
- [ ] An approval raised on one channel cannot be answered from another
- [ ] Expiry is enforced by the clock, not by a message
- [ ] Every approval leaves an audit line naming session, channel and outcome

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/approval.test.js test/agent.test.js
```

## Time estimate

~1 week

items.title: feat(skills): a portable, verifiable skill file others can run and check
items.body:
## Context

A category leader does not only keep its knowledge in a database. If a compiled skill cannot leave the machine, every user starts from zero and no one can check anyone's work. A small, plain-text, signed-by-content skill file — preconditions, steps, verification steps, and the corpus it was measured on — turns a personal routine into something a colleague can review, run and reject.

## What to change

- A versioned JSON skill file: trigger phrases, preconditions, steps with argument templates, a verification step per action and the provenance (trace id, date, machine).
- Import that re-runs verification before the skill is accepted, and refuses a skill whose steps include an unverified or dangerous action.
- A content hash, so a shared skill can be compared and a mutated one is visibly different.
- `node scripts/skill.js verify <file>` for a reviewer who does not trust the sender.

**Safety:** importing a skill is not importing permission: a portable skill still runs through this machine's approval gate, and a skill cannot embed a pre-approved action.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — skills do not exist yet outside the roadmap; nothing is exportable, importable or checkable
- **Target:** export/import round-trips byte-identically, 100% of imports with a missing precondition list or a dangerous step are refused, and `verify` runs in 2 seconds or less per skill
- **Must not regress:** must not regress replay determinism or the approval gate, and must not accept a skill whose content hash does not match its steps

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A skill exported on one machine imports on another with identical steps
- [ ] A tampered skill fails its hash check with a specific message
- [ ] A skill containing a shell step is refused without an explicit override
- [ ] Verification runs offline, with no network access

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/skill.test.js
node scripts/skill.js verify test-fixtures/skills/example.json
```

## Time estimate

~1.5 weeks

items.title: test(eval): a labelled conversation corpus that scores answering, not uptime
items.body:
## Context

This repository measures retrieval (`pinch-022`), the deterministic fast path (`mind-01`), the laptop control floor (`lead-06`) and readiness (`pinch-012`). It does not measure the thing the product is for: whether an answer was right.

Every serious assistant stack now ships an eval loop, and the ones that compound quality do it without a vendor: a versioned corpus, a deterministic runner, per-class scores, and a rule that a regression names the failing cases. Without it, every speed item in this roadmap is unmeasurable on the axis that matters most — `mind-03`'s "equal or better task success" is currently a sentence with nothing behind it.

## What to change

- A corpus of 60 turns across six classes: factual lookup with a citation, document question with an unanswerable variant, multi-turn follow-up ("the second one"), tool-needed, refusal/abstain, and a short social turn. Each carries the expected answer shape, not the expected wording.
- A scorer with two layers: deterministic checks (citation resolves to a retrieved source, no invented file path, no claim of an action that did not run, tool used when required) and an optional local-model judge for answer adequacy, recorded with model id, seed and prompt hash so a score can be reproduced.
- One command, offline, in under five minutes, printing per-class scores and a single score with the commit it ran against.
- The judge prompt is versioned like code; a change to it changes the score and must be reviewed as such.
- `docs/CONVERSATION.md`: what is scored, what is deliberately not (style, verbosity), and the honest limit — a local judge is a weak judge, so deterministic checks carry the gate.

**Safety:** the corpus is synthetic and local — no user conversation is ever used as eval data, nothing is uploaded, and the judge runs on the configured local model. Scoring must not require the network, so the gate works on a plane.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — the repo scores retrieval, the fast path and readiness, but no test measures whether an answer was correct, cited or coherent (0 answer-quality assertions in the suite)
- **Target:** 60 labelled turns scored offline in **under 5 minutes**, producing a reproducible single score with per-class breakdown, of which at least 30 turns are gated by deterministic checks rather than a model judge
- **Must not regress:** the bench must not become a benchmark nobody runs: it stays inside the five-minute CI budget, and a score change must name the failing turn ids instead of printing a smaller number

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The corpus is versioned, synthetic and committed with the harness
- [ ] Deterministic checks gate at least 30 turns; the judge is optional and recorded

items.title: feat(rag): decide dense retrieval and reranking on the labelled corpus, not on fashion
items.verify:
node --test test/documents.test.js test/retrieval-evaluation.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
items.body:
## Context

`src/documents.js` is a zero-dependency BM25 index, which is the right starting point and the wrong finishing point: BM25 cannot answer a question phrased in words the document does not use. Every local assistant that is good at documents adds a second retriever and fuses by rank.

The published gains are real but smaller and more conditional than the marketing suggests: tuned hybrid fusion on WANDS gave +7.4% NDCG over either retriever alone; a financial-document bench moved recall@5 from 0.644 (BM25) to 0.695 (RRF) and to 0.816 with a cross-encoder rerank. Against that, one public implementation measured reranking at **+0.8% NDCG for 20x the latency**. Reranking is not free and is not automatically a win — which is why this item is a gate, not a build order.

## What to change

- Measure first: run the existing corpus (`pinch-022`) through BM25 alone, then BM25 + a dense retriever fused with reciprocal rank fusion, then fused + a small local reranker over the top 20.
- Adopt each stage only if it earns its latency on the corpus; publish the negative result when it does not, and keep the simpler index.
- Embeddings are computed locally and cached with the document's content hash, so re-indexing a changed file does not re-embed the library.
- `docs/RETRIEVAL-EVALUATION.md`: the per-stage table (recall@5, nDCG@10, p50/p95) and the explicit decision this item produced.

**Safety:** retrieval stays local: any embedding model runs on the machine, and no document text may be sent to a provider. The index remains a plain local file, and a cache miss must degrade to BM25 rather than to a network call.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** BM25 only — one retriever, no fusion, no reranker; recall@5 and nDCG@10 are measured by `pinch-022` and every improvement is unquantified until this item runs
- **Target:** recall@5 up **8 percentage points or more** on the committed corpus at **p95 <= 150 ms** total retrieval, with each added stage individually justified in the results table
- **Must not regress:** an added stage that does not clear both bars must be removed rather than left enabled "for the future"; citation correctness may not drop; no retrieval path may require the network

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The corpus report contains BM25, hybrid and hybrid+rerank rows with recall@5, nDCG@10 and p50/p95
- [ ] Every stage adopted clears 8 pp recall@5 at p95 <= 150 ms, or is rejected in writing
- [ ] Embedding cache is keyed by content hash and re-indexing an unchanged vault is fast
- [ ] Citations still resolve to real passages after fusion and reranking
- [ ] Zero network calls on the retrieval path, asserted by test

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/documents.test.js test/retrieval-evaluation.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
```

## Time estimate

~1-2 weeks

items.title: feat(rag): abstain instead of asserting what the retrieved passage does not say
items.verify:
node --test test/citations.test.js test/guard.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
items.body:
## Context

`src/guard.js` audits claims the assistant makes about **actions** — it will not let a reply say a file was written when the write failed. Nothing audits claims about **sources**. A document answer can cite a real passage and still say something the passage does not say, and the panel shows a tidy `[1]` next to a wrong sentence.

Assistants that lead on trust handle this with a check-and-abstain step: for each sentence that carries a citation, decide whether the cited span supports it, and when it does not, either widen the citation or say it could not find the answer. "I could not find that in your notes" is a better answer than a confident fabrication with a footnote.

## What to change

- Extract citation-bearing sentences from the answer and the retrieved span each one points at.
- A cheap local support check, deterministic first: does the cited span contain the named entity and the number/date the sentence asserts? Lexical entailment catches the common failure (right document, wrong figure) without a model call.
- An optional single local-model pass for what the lexical check cannot decide, bounded to the cited sentences and never to the whole reply.
- Three outcomes rendered honestly: supported (citation kept), unsupported (citation dropped and the sentence softened or removed), unanswerable (explicit abstain, with the searched locations listed).
- `docs/GUIDE.md`: what a citation means here, now that it means "this span supports this sentence".

**Safety:** the check may only *reduce* confidence. It can remove a citation or replace a claim with an abstain; it can never be used to add a citation, to reword a claim into something the source does not support, or to skip the action gate.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** not implemented — citations are attached by retrieval, not verified against the sentence; 0 checks compare a claim with the span it cites
- **Target:** unsupported cited sentences down **50% or more** on the committed corpus with abstain precision at **90% or more** (an abstain must be correct), for **<= 150 ms** added latency on document answers
- **Must not regress:** answers that were already correct must not start abstaining; a supported claim may not be softened; a citation may never be invented to satisfy the checker; non-document turns are untouched

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Lexical support check runs with no model call and catches the wrong-figure case in the corpus
- [ ] Unsupported rate halves; abstain precision is measured, not assumed
- [ ] A supported answer keeps its citation verbatim
- [ ] The abstain text names what was searched and says the answer was not found
- [ ] Added latency stays at or below 150 ms on document turns
- [ ] Non-document turns show no behaviour change

## How to verify

```bash
node --test test/citations.test.js test/guard.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
```

## Time estimate

~1-2 weeks

items.title: perf(memory): recall the facts that matter, not the last forty
items.verify:
node --test test/agent.test.js test/router.test.js
node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js
items.body:
## Context

`src/prompt.js` injects `loadMemory().facts.slice(-40)` into the system prompt and `slice(-8)` into the conversation prompt. That is recency, not relevance: after a month of use the assistant carries forty mostly-unrelated facts on every turn, which dilutes attention, costs prefill, and changes the prompt prefix so often that caching (`mind-04`) cannot help.

Memory systems that work rank and bound by relevance, keep pinned facts always present, and — the part usually skipped — record where a fact came from so a wrong one can be corrected rather than accumulating. `harness-05` covers provenance; this item covers selection.

## What to change

- Rank remembered facts against the current turn using the existing local scorer (`src/documents.js` BM25 is already in the tree) plus a pinned set and a recency tiebreak.
- A token budget for the memory block rather than a count of facts, so a fact with a long body cannot crowd out five short ones.
- Pinned facts (name, timezone, preferences the owner marked) always included; unpinned facts included only when they score above a floor, with the floor measured rather than guessed.
- The block goes **after** the static prefix (see `mind-04`), so relevance selection and cache reuse do not fight each other.
- Recall quality measured on a labelled set of turns: did the fact the turn needed make the cut?

**Safety:** no fact may be sent anywhere, no new store, and nothing is deleted: this changes what is *included* in a prompt, never what is remembered. A fact that fails to be recalled is still there next turn.

## Performance contract

- **Baseline:** recency only — up to 40 facts are injected into the system prompt and 8 into the conversation prompt by position, with 0 relevance scoring and no token budget for the block
- **Target:** injected memory tokens down **60% or more** on turns where more than 20 facts are stored, while recall@5 of the needed fact stays at **90% or more** on the labelled turn set
- **Must not regress:** the fact a turn needs may not stop being available; pinned facts may never be dropped; a 90%-recall result may not be reached by simply injecting everything again

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Memory injection has a token budget and a measured relevance floor
- [ ] Pinned facts are always present; unpinned facts must earn their place
- [ ] recall@5 of the needed fact is 90% or more on the labelled turns
- [ ] Injected memory tokens drop 60% or more on fact-heavy turns
- [ ] Nothing is deleted from the store by this change
- [ ] The memory block sits after the static prefix and does not break `mind-04`'s cache test

## How to verify

node --test --test-concurrency=4 && node scripts/audit.js

~4-6 days
